newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Petrol price war seen looming in South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Petrol price war seen looming in South Korea.

text.p: Petrol prices are coming down at South Korean pumps in what some industry analysts described on Thursday as the start of a price war.
Prices were deregulated on January 1, sparking increases over the following two months.

But with the cost of crude oil imports now falling, the nation's biggest refiners are dropping their prices. Refiners say cheaper petrol will eat into profits, but some analysts believe refiners can afford to keep consumers happy.
"It's the start of a price war," said Lee Sang-koo, an energy analyst at Hyundai Securities.
The last time South Korean refiners engaged in cut-throat competition, in 1994, the whole industry suffered.
But Bill Hunsaker, an energy analyst at ING-Barings Securities, said he did not believe refiners were about to make the same mistake.
"I wouldn't call it a price war," he said. "I'd say price competition has increased."

All major refiners brought down their prices on Tuesday, but Ssangyong Oil Refining Co and Hanwha Energy Co Ltd made the steepest cuts, setting prices at 832 won (93 cents) and 831 won per litre respectively.
After Yukong Ltd, LG-Caltex Oil Corp and Hyundai Oil Refinery Co realised their prices were out of line, they chopped their rates again on Wednesday.
Hyundai lowered its retail petrol price to 832 won (93 cents) a litre on Wednesday from 842 won announced on Tuesday, Yukong to 837 won from 843 won and LG-Caltex to 839-840 won from 843 won.
Prices last month averaged 845-846 won.
"To keep market share, we had no choice but to follow Ssangyong and Hanwha's move and additionally cut our petrol prices," said a Hyundai Oil official.
"Price cuts will hurt our profits, already hit by the Korean won's depreciation against the dollar," he said. The won has fallen six percent so far this year and on Thursday closed at 894.70.
Profits of South Korean refiners were savaged last year, largely as a result of foreign exchange losses.
"Refiners are cutting prices because they can afford to," said Hunsaker. He said refiners could subsidise further price cuts by raising other product prices.
Industry analysts said LG-Caltex, Yukong and Hyundai were worst placed to cut petrol prices. Those companies are burdened with debt as a result of huge facility expansion.
Last year, Hyundai and Yukong added 200,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) refining capacity each and LG-Caltex 220,000 bpd.
Analysts said it was difficult to say whether any refiner would gain from a price war.

A round of vicious price-cutting in 1994 was sparked by Ssangyong's effort to secure greater market share regardless of profit. Ssangyong's market share rose slightly at first, but fell back after several months.
Some analysts pointed out that market conditions had changed since 1994. Consumers were now far more price sensitive and were likely to switch brand for small savings.
"Customers could respond more favourably because of the current economic hardship and higher cost of living," said Lee of Hyundai.
